orders.description: Plaintiffs’ appeal from the order granting defendant summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff tripped in the lower parking lot on defendant’s premises during spring. Her deposition errata clarified that she believed loose or broken blacktop caused the fall; photographs may show vegetation through the surface.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied reasonable maintenance through noncreation and lack of notice; defendant failed the constructive-notice showing.
Noncreation appears in the governing burden; the application does not separately resolve who created the broken-surface condition.
The owner described lack of actual notice, but the decision rests on inadequate constructive-notice proof rather than a separate conclusive actual-notice finding.
Possible longstanding deterioration and missing inspection/resurfacing timing defeated defendant’s initial showing. Constructive notice was conditional on duration, not conclusively found.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition and errata described the trip material; defendant’s owner gave general maintenance testimony without relevant inspection or resurfacing timing.
Photographs may show vegetation through the lot surface and support possible longstanding deterioration; no independent image inspection is claimed.

quality.notes: Defendant’s premises and business maintenance support private lot control, without assuming title from the witness being an owner of the company. Do not infer restaurant use from kitchen-help wording. Spring is the only accident timing; date remains null. Errata clarification is retained, not silently substituted for the original gravel account. Snow plowing was expressly unrelated, and grass-cutting testimony did not locate the grass near the lots. Plaintiff’s role is unstated.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and motion denied.
Plaintiff Belinda McNally (hereinafter plaintiff) tripped and fell while walking in the lower parking lot on defendant’s premises.
Following discovery, defendant moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint. Supreme Court granted the motion. Plaintiffs appeal.

A landowner meets its prima facie burden of establishing that it fulfilled its duty to maintain its property in a reasonably safe condition by showing that it did not create a dangerous or defective condition and did not have actual or constructive notice of such a condition

Here, defendant submitted the deposition transcript of one of its owners, as well as plaintiffs deposition transcript. Although the owner testified generally regarding maintenance of the parking lots and the lack of any actual notice, he did not establish a lack of constructive notice.
Plaintiff testified that the parking lot contained chunks of blacktop that appeared loose and broken, and that she believed that she tripped on a piece of this broken blacktop.
The record also contains photographs that may show weeds or grass growing through the parking lot’s surface.

the condition of the parking lot indicates that it may not have been properly maintained for some time. If the condition existed for an extended time, such that defendant could have discovered and remedied it, defendant had constructive notice of a defective condition

But when asked when the parking lots were last resurfaced prior to plaintiffs fall, he could not recall. Other than mentioning snow plowing, which was not in any way involved in this springtime incident, the owner did not testify that he or any of his co-owners or employees maintained or inspected the parking lots.
He did not even mention when anyone on behalf of defendant had previously been to or looked at the lower parking lot or the ramp leading to it.

Due to defendant’s failure to submit any evidence that it lacked constructive notice of the condition of the parking lots, which plaintiffs testimony indicated was dangerous due to the chunks of broken blacktop, defendant failed to meet its burden of demonstrating its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law
Thus, we need not address the sufficiency of plaintiffs’ proof in response; defendant’s motion for summary judgment should have been denied

Although plaintiff originally testified that the parking lot consisted of a composite of different materials and she tripped on gravel, her errata sheet clarifies that she believed that she tripped on “chunks of blacktop” or “loose and broken blacktop.”

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the April 13, 2015 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a wet floor inside defendants’ building after rain. A doorman described no wetness 40 minutes earlier, and the record concerned mopping, a gap between a mat and stairs, and incomplete preservation of surveillance video.

legal_issues.finding: No continuous mopping or complete mat coverage was required, but absent accident-day mopping evidence and the mat/stair gap left adequacy of precautions triable.
The court identifies disputed notice without separately deciding actual knowledge; the doorman’s account and missing video did not justify judgment.
Notice remained triable despite the doorman’s 40-minute account; missing video and inadequate evidence of accident-day precautions prevented dismissal.
Failure to preserve the entire video defeated summary judgment in these circumstances; whether to impose a particular sanction remained for trial.
The prior video-production order denied without prejudice had no preclusive effect.

evidence_discussed.description: Doorman described dry conditions 40 minutes earlier; general rainy-day mopping testimony did not establish mopping that day.
The complete relevant video was not preserved; the opinion addresses that loss rather than a conclusive account from footage. No independent playback occurred.

quality.notes: Building attribution, doorman and cleaning practices do not expressly establish private ownership/lease or building use; retain property review under existing rules rather than infer from the corporate name. This is substantive notice/precautions review with ancillary spoliation, not procedural-only. No specific sanction or intentional destruction is conclusively found. Only the current denial order is independently appealed; the prior production order is history. Plaintiff’s role and accident date are unstated; no inference links death in the caption to the fall.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Alison Y. Tuitt, J.), entered April 13, 2015, which denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.

In this action alleging a slip and fall on a wet floor inside defendants' building shortly after it had been raining, triable issues of fact exist as to defendants' claimed lack of notice and their precautions in light of the dangerous condition.

Even though the building doorman testified that there was no wet condition when he left for lunch 40 minutes before the accident, the building's "either . . . negligent or willful" failure to preserve the entire surveillance video of the area where plaintiff slipped and fell is sufficient under the circumstances of this case to defeat summary judgement at this time, with the specific spoliation sanction, if any, to be determined at trial
Contrary to the defendant's contention, the court's prior order regarding production of the entire surveillance video, which was denied without prejudice, has no preclusive effect.
Although defendants were not required to mop continuously, and there was testimony that they usually mopped when it rained, there was no evidence that they mopped at all on the day of the accident

Furthermore, while defendants were not required to cover the entire floor with mats, under the facts of this case the gap between the mat and the stairs raised an issue of fact as to the adequacy of defendants' precautions.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the December 2, 2010 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on snow and ice on a driveway parking-lot ramp at defendant’s premises on February 12, 2008. A nonparty described preexisting icy patches in the lot and ramps generally.

legal_issues.finding: Noncreation was part of the initial burden, satisfied here through storm evidence; no separate negligent snow-removal or creation theory was analyzed.
General nearby ice evidence did not raise a triable issue of actual notice of the specific preexisting condition at the fall site.
Pre-storm ice in the vicinity was insufficient to raise constructive notice of the specific accident-area condition.
Defendant established an ongoing storm; plaintiff failed to raise a triable preexisting-condition/notice exception at the specific fall site.
Plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue that a sufficiently noticed pre-storm condition, rather than current precipitation, caused the accident.

evidence_discussed.description: Nonparty sworn statement described icy patches generally, insufficient to establish the relevant specific-site notice issue.

quality.notes: The parking ramp is expressly at defendant’s premises, supporting private lot control, without inferring legal title or residential use from the name. Location other denotes the ramp rather than a stairway or public road. Plaintiff’s role is unstated. The storm proof’s format is unspecified, so no meteorological records or expert report is invented. A cited case against the same defendant does not establish a duplicate or shared incident.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.

The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries he allegedly sustained on February 12, 2008, when he slipped and fell on snow and ice on a driveway parking lot ramp at the defendant’s premises.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (McDonald, J.), dated December 2, 2010, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

As the proponent of the motion for summary judgment, the defendant had to establish, prima facie, that it neither created the snow and ice condition nor had actual or constructive notice of the condition
Here, the defendant sustained this burden by presenting evidence that there was a storm in progress when the plaintiff fell

To do so, the plaintiff was required to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether the accident was caused by a slippery condition at the location where the plaintiff fell that existed prior to the storm, as opposed to precipitation from the storm in progress, and that the defendant had actual or constructive notice of the preexisting condition
Here, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact in this regard.
The sworn statement of a nonparty witness merely referred to the existence of icy patches within the parking lot, including the exit and entry ramps.

Evidence that there was ice in the general vicinity of the accident prior to the storm is insufficient to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether the defendant had actual or constructive notice of the condition of the specific area within the parking lot where the plaintiff fell
Therefore, the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint should have been granted.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the November 1, 2018 order granting summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff, an occupational therapy assistant leaving a client at defendant’s group home, allegedly slipped on its asphalt driveway. The alleged condition consisted of numerous cracks.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the reasonably-safe-premises duty, with defendant failing its initial causation, notice and triviality showings.
Noncreation appears in the governing burden; no separate finding resolves who caused the driveway cracks.
Lack of actual notice appears in the governing rule; the application specifically resolves constructive-notice deficiency, not actual knowledge.
General practices and an inspection about seven weeks earlier did not establish a sufficiently recent inspection of the accident area.
Defendant failed to establish that the cracked condition was trivial as a matter of law.
Defendant’s own submissions, including plaintiff’s deposition, left triable issues whether driveway cracks caused the slip.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted plaintiff’s deposition; it did not eliminate cracked-driveway causation issues.
Employee affidavits described general/monthly inspection practices and a seven-week-old inspection; these were insufficient for lack of constructive notice.

quality.notes: Express ownership/operation supports private group-home premises; institutional describes the group-home setting without inferring public ownership or nonprofit status. Plaintiff’s work-related visit does not establish employment by defendant or an independent-contractor relationship, so role is other. Driveway is location other, not an invented parking lot. No accident date is stated. Employee affidavits are not inspection records, and initial-burden failure is not established negligence.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.
The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries that she alleges she sustained when she fell on the driveway of a group home owned and operated by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Dutchess County (Edward T. McLoughlin, J.), dated November 1, 2018. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
According to the plaintiff, she is a certified occupational therapy assistant and had just left one of her clients who resided in the group home when she slipped and fell on the asphalt driveway.
A property owner has a duty to maintain its premises in a reasonably safe condition
a defendant real property owner generally must establish, prima facie, that it neither created the allegedly dangerous or defective condition nor had actual or constructive notice of its existence

the defendant failed to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff could not identify the cause of her fall. The evidence submitted by the defendant, which included a transcript of the plaintiff's deposition testimony, failed to eliminate all triable issues of fact as to whether the numerous cracks that constituted the condition of the driveway had caused the plaintiff to fall
The defendant also failed to establish, prima facie, that it did not have constructive notice of the alleged hazardous condition of the driveway

The affidavit of the defendant's maintenance worker submitted in support of the defendant's motion referred only to his general inspection practices but did not refer to any specific inspection in the area of the plaintiff's fall relative to the date of the incident.

Another employee of the defendant averred in an affidavit that she had inspected the driveway approximately seven weeks prior to the plaintiff's fall and found all routes were clear of obstructions. She also averred that the defendant's maintenance department inspected the driveway at least once per month. This evidence was insufficient to establish, prima facie, lack of constructive notice
The defendant failed to establish, prima facie, that the cracked condition of the driveway was trivial as a matter of law, and thus, nonactionable
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, without regard to the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the August 5, 2016 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff fell when a brick moved beneath him on the exterior landing at his apartment building. He had placed bricks there to negotiate an allegedly high doorway step; plaintiffs also alleged missing or blocked handrails.

legal_issues.finding: The landlords had assumed repair duties and reserved entry rights; the decision applied the duty to remedy noticed dangerous conditions.
Defendants relied on plaintiff’s brick placement as creation of the hazard, but that did not eliminate factual issues about foreseeable consequences of their alleged premises negligence.
Defendants’ awareness of the high step, handrail problems and plaintiff’s brick placement was undisputed.
Constructive notice appears in the allegations and governing burden, but the application relies on undisputed awareness rather than a separate constructive-notice finding.
Defendants raised this defense for the first time on appeal; the court rejected its consideration as unpreserved without reaching its merits.
Defendants did not establish that brick placement was a superseding intervening cause, rather than a normal or foreseeable consequence of alleged premises negligence.
Defendants raised this defense for the first time on appeal; the court rejected its consideration as unpreserved without reaching its merits.
Assumption-of-risk and obviousness arguments were improperly raised for the first time on appeal, not resolved on their merits.

evidence_discussed.description: Complaint and bill of particulars described the high step, brick placement and missing/blocked handrails; specific testimony or evidentiary formats are not identified.

quality.notes: A personal fall on a moving brick is explicit, but whether that mechanism constitutes a slip/trip rather than another displacement-of-support fall is unresolved under the current codebook. Retain review, not a definite nonfall exclusion. Private apartment ownership and landlord/leased-residence context establish tenant status. Landing at the doorway is entrance; the actual fall is not asserted to be on a stair tread. Superseding-cause analysis is not a comparative-fault allocation. No out-of-possession status follows solely from reserved entry. Accident date is unstated.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.

Memorandum: Plaintiffs commenced this action seeking damages for injuries allegedly arising from an incident in which Laszlo Biro (plaintiff) stepped on one of several bricks or blocks (hereafter, bricks) that he had placed on an exterior landing of an apartment building owned by defendants, where plaintiffs resided, and he fell when the brick moved.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Steuben County (Joseph W. Latham, A.J.), dated August 5, 2016. The order denied the motion of defendants for summary judgment.

In the complaint, as amplified by the bill of particulars, plaintiffs alleged that the incident was caused by several dangerous conditions on the premises, including that the step from the landing to the doorway was too high, that plaintiff was forced to place bricks on the landing to permit plaintiffs to enter and exit the apartment, that there was no hand rail on one side of the door, that defendants installed a screen door that blocked the hand rail on the other side of the door, and that defendants had actual and constructive notice of those conditions but failed to remedy them.

Defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending that plaintiff created the dangerous condition on the premises by placing the bricks on the landing, and that plaintiff's conduct was a superseding intervening act that was the sole proximate cause of the accident.

It is well settled that "a landlord may be found liable for failure to repair a dangerous condition, of which it has notice, on leased premises [where, as here,] the landlord assumes a duty to make repairs and reserves the right to enter in order to inspect or to make such repairs"
Here, it is undisputed that defendants were aware of the high step, as well as the missing and blocked hand rails, and that plaintiff had placed the bricks on the landing under the door.

We agree with the court, however, that defendants failed to eliminate all triable issues of fact whether plaintiff's conduct in placing the bricks on the landing was a superseding intervening cause of the accident, i.e., defendants failed to meet their burden of establishing that the accident was not "a normal or foreseeable consequence of the situation created by [their] [alleged] negligence"
Inasmuch as defendants failed to establish their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the court properly denied the motion, regardless of the sufficiency of the opposing papers
Finally, defendants' further contentions, which concern assumption of the risk and the allegedly open and obvious nature of the dangerous condition, are improperly raised for the first time on appeal

"Thus, in a premises liability case, a defendant property owner who moves for summary judgment has the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that it neither created the defective condition nor had actual or constructive notice of its existence"
